answer: I would like to describe a former colleague who once solved a tricky problem at work in a genuinely clever way. He worked with me at the education consultancy until last year, when he left to do a master's degree in Australia. Our team was stuck on a project because of a scheduling conflict that seemed impossible to resolve. We had organised a university fair, but two of the most popular universities could only send representatives at exactly the same time, and we had only one hall big enough for the crowds we were expecting. While the rest of us were arguing, he calmly suggested a completely different approach that none of us had considered. He proposed dividing the hall with screens and running both sessions side by side. What impressed me was how [[resourceful]] he was; he found a simple solution hidden in plain sight. His thinking was refreshingly [[lateral]], approaching the problem from an angle nobody else had tried. Within an hour, something that had frustrated us for days was neatly sorted out, and the fair went smoothly. As for how I felt, I was relieved but also slightly embarrassed that I had not thought of it myself. I think his real strength is staying calm and [[rational]] when everyone else is panicking. That episode taught me that the best solutions are often surprisingly simple, once someone [[ingenious]] points them out. Honestly, I still think about his approach whenever I feel stuck on a difficult problem myself.

followUps.q: Are you good at solving problems?
followUps.answer: Reasonably good, I think, especially practical ones. I tend to be methodical rather than creative, so I break problems into steps. I have learned, though, that stepping away for a while often brings a [[breakthrough]].

followUps.q: Do you think problem-solving skills can be taught?
followUps.answer: Yes, to some extent. Schools can encourage it by giving students open-ended tasks instead of memorisation. But experience is the best teacher, because real problems rarely come with clear instructions.

note: Set him at my consultancy, made the problem concrete (two universities, one hall at a fair), explained his solution and how I felt.
